In the Nxeon codebase at /opt/nxeon (Next.js 15 App Router + TypeScript + Prisma + Postgres), I need a thorough understanding of the CURRENT auth/role/admin-access-control system, to plan adding: (a) new staff roles beyond ADMIN/CUSTOMER, (b) granular per-page/per-section admin access control, (c) a separate employee-facing portal, (d) per-staff IP whitelisting.

Investigate and report on:
1. The `User` model in prisma/schema.prisma — the `Role` enum's exact values, and any other role/permission-related fields (look for anything like `role`, `area`, `permissions`, `canAccess`).
2. `lib/auth.ts` — how `requireUser()`/`requireAdmin()` work, how the session cookie works, whether there's an "impersonation" mechanism, and whether there's any existing IP-based restriction anywhere in the codebase (grep for "ipHash", "clientIp", "allowlist", "whitelist", "IP restrict").
3. Search for `canAccess` and `requireArea` (mentioned in a comment I recall as "Fleet/admin RBAC via requireArea('fleet')") — find their definitions and EVERY distinct "area" string used across the admin codebase (grep for `requireArea(` and `canAccess(` calls) — this tells us what granularity of admin-page access control ALREADY exists today, which is critical: is there already a real per-section admin permission system I should extend, or is it just a flat ADMIN vs CUSTOMER boolean with a couple of hardcoded areas?
4. `app/admin/layout.tsx` (or wherever the admin portal's own layout/nav lives) — how the admin nav is built, whether it already varies by role/area, and the full list of admin page destinations that exist today (grep the admin nav array).
5. The `AuditLog` model and how audit logging currently works (`lib/actions.ts`'s `audit()` helper or wherever it lives) — what actions currently get logged, and whether there's an admin UI to VIEW audit logs (e.g. is there an /admin/activity or /admin/audit page already?).
6. Whether a "Discord staff OAuth" or similar staff-identity-linking system already exists (I recall a `discordUserId` field on User and a "Discord staff OAuth" feature) — read enough to understand how staff members are currently identified/authenticated today, since this may already be half of what's needed for a broader staff-identity system.
7. The specific admin pages mentioned by the user: search for admin routes related to "tickets" (support), "reddit" (Reddit marketing templates), "inbox"/"mail" (admin-side mail), "mailboxes", and "clients"/"customers" (an admin customer-list page) — find their exact file paths under app/admin/, and how each currently gates access (just `requireAdmin()`, or something more granular).

Report back with: exact file paths and line numbers for everything above, the exact Role enum values, the exact list of "area" strings already in use for requireArea if that system exists, and a clear statement of whether per-page admin access control already exists in some form or would be entirely new. Keep the report well-organized and focused — this is feeding directly into an implementation plan.

- figma:figma-create-new-file: **MANDATORY prerequisite** — you MUST invoke this skill BEFORE every `create_new_file` tool call. NEVER call `create_new_file` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user wants a new blank Figma file — a new design, FigJam, or Slides file — or when you need a fresh file before calling `use_figma`. Example prompts (not exhaustive) are 'implement this Figma design', 'build this screen from Figma', 'turn this Figma into code', 'design to code'. This skill provides critical instructions and steps to the agent on how to correctly implement Figma designs in code and must NOT be skipped.
- figma:figma-generate-design: Use this skill alongside figma-use when the task involves translating an application page, view, or multi-section layout into Figma. Triggers: 'write to Figma', 'create in Figma from code', 'push page to Figma', 'take this app/page and build it in Figma', 'create a screen', 'build a landing page in Figma', 'update the Figma screen to match code', 'convert this modal/dialog/drawer/panel to Figma'. This is the preferred workflow skill whenever the user wants to build or update a full page, modal, dialog, drawer, sidebar, panel, or any composed multi-section view in Figma from code or a description. Discovers design system components, variables, and styles from Code Connect files, existing screens, and library search, then imports them and assembles views incrementally section-by-section using design system tokens instead of hardcoded values.
- figma:figma-generate-diagram: MANDATORY prerequisite — load this skill BEFORE every `generate_diagram` tool call. NEVER call `generate_diagram` directly without loading this skill first. Trigger whenever the user asks to create, generate, draw, render, sketch, or build a diagram — flowchart, architecture diagram, sequence diagram, ERD or entity-relationship diagram, state diagram or state machine, gantt chart, or timeline. Also trigger when the user mentions Mermaid syntax or wants a system architecture, decision tree, dependency graph, API call flow, auth handshake, schema, or pipeline visualized in FigJam. Routes to type-specific guidance, sets universal Mermaid constraints, and tells you when to use a different diagram type or skip the tool entirely (mindmaps, pie charts, class diagrams, etc.).

Use when the user wants to create variables/tokens, build component libraries, create individual components with proper variant sets and variable bindings, set up theming (light/dark modes), document foundations, or reconcile gaps between code and Figma. Also use when the user asks to create or generate any component in Figma — even a single one — since components require proper variable foundations, variant states, and design token bindings to be production-quality. This skill teaches WHAT to build and in WHAT ORDER — it complements the `figma-use` skill which teaches HOW to call the Plugin API. Both skills should be loaded together.
- figma:figma-implement-motion: Translates Figma motion and animations into production-ready application code. Use when implementing animation/motion from a Figma design — user mentions "implement this motion", "add animation from Figma", "animate this component", provides a Figma URL whose node is animated, or when `get_design_context` returns motion data or instructs you to call `get_motion_context`.

- anthropic-skills:docx: Use this skill whenever the user wants to create, read, edit, or manipulate Word documents (.docx) or Word templates (.dotx). Triggers include: any mention of 'Word doc', 'word document', '.docx', '.dotx', or requests to produce professional documents with formatting like tables of contents, page numbers, or letterheads. - anthropic-skills:import-memory: Import a memory export from another AI assistant into Claude's memory — conversationally, additively, and with the content treated as data.

Use only when the user explicitly asks to run, see, or set up their morning brief, or if they invoke /morning by name. A question about their day, schedule, or calendar is not by itself a request for the brief; answer it directly instead.
- anthropic-skills:pdf: Use this skill whenever the user wants to do anything with PDF files. This includes reading or extracting text/tables from PDFs, combining or merging multiple PDFs into one, splitting PDFs apart, rotating pages, adding watermarks, creating new PDFs, filling PDF forms, encrypting/decrypting PDFs, extracting images, and OCR on scanned PDFs to make them searchable. If the user mentions a .pdf file or asks to produce one, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:pptx: Use this skill any time a .pptx or .potx file is involved in any way — as input, output, or both. This includes: creating slide decks, pitch decks, or presentations as PowerPoint (.pptx) files; reading, parsing, or extracting text from any .pptx or .potx file (even if the extracted content will be used elsewhere, like in an email, summary, or creating a different type of slide deck); editing, modifying, or updating existing presentations; combining or splitting slide files; working with templates (.potx), layouts, speaker notes, or comments. Trigger whenever the user asks for a PowerPoint or .pptx file, or references a .pptx or .potx filename, regardless of what they plan to do with the content afterward. However, when the user asks for a deck, slides, a slide deck, or a presentation without naming a file format, default to using a dedicated slide-deck artifact type or a separate slides skill if this session offers one; otherwise, use this skill.
- anthropic-skills:schedule: Create or update a scheduled task that runs automatically. Use when the user says things like "every day", "each morning", "remind me in an hour", "run this at noon", or wants to reschedule an existing task.
- anthropic-skills:setup-cowork: Guided Cowork setup — install role-matched plugins, connect your tools, try a skill.
- anthropic-skills:skill-creator: Create new skills, modify and improve existing skills, and measure skill performance. Use when users want to create a skill from scratch, edit, or optimize an existing skill, run evals to test a skill, benchmark skill performance with variance analysis, or optimize a skill's description for better triggering accuracy.
- anthropic-skills:xlsx: Use this skill any time a spreadsheet file is the primary input or output. This means any task where the user wants to: open, read, edit, or fix an existing .xlsx, .xlsm, .xltx, .csv, or .tsv file (e.g., adding columns, computing formulas, formatting, charting, cleaning messy data); create a new spreadsheet from scratch or from other data sources; or convert between tabular file formats. Trigger especially when the user references a spreadsheet file by name or path — even casually (like "the xlsx in my downloads") — and wants something done to it or produced from it. Also trigger for cleaning or restructuring messy tabular data files (malformed rows, misplaced headers, junk data) into proper spreadsheets. The deliverable must be a spreadsheet file. Do NOT trigger when the primary deliverable is a Word document, HTML report, standalone Python script, database pipeline, or Google Sheets API integration, even if tabular data is involved.
- design: Create a design canvas - a multi-artboard visual design published as an Artifact that runs Claude Design's canvas editor (an early preview of Claude Design inside Claude Code). You DRAFT the design as .dc.html artboards laid out on one pan/zoom canvas; where saving is enabled for the user's account they refine every element visually (click-to-select, a properties panel, inline text editing, undo/redo) and Save publishes a new version for everyone, otherwise they get a view-and-export (PNG/PDF) preview of your draft. Good for UI mockups and screen flows, landing pages, marketing and social graphics, and print pieces - posters, flyers, brochures as single-page artboards; memos and reports as one flowing artboard. Use when someone wants a design, mockup, wireframe, UI or screen design, landing page, poster, flyer, brochure, banner, card, one-pager, or any visual layout they would rather tweak by hand than in code. Only for CREATING or re-seeding a canvas; an existing one is edited in its published Artifact.
- dataviz: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Read it BEFORE writing the first line of chart code, choosing chart colors, building a stat tile / meter / KPI row, or laying out a dashboard. When the destination is a first-party document connector (host-designated, never self-described) that renders live charts, hand it the rows (inline, or as an uploaded data file the chart cites) rather than a rendered PNG/SVG — a picture of a chart loses hover, data inspection and per-value comments. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Triggers on: "chart", "graph", "plot", "data viz", "visualization", "dashboard", "analytics", "visualize data", "categorical colors", "sequential / diverging palette", "stat tile", "sparkline", "heatmap", "legend", "axis", "tooltip", "chart colors", "color by series".
- artifact-design: Design guidance and fundamentals for Artifacts. - Load before writing any artifact, including a skill-instructed Markdown one - Markdown is never a shortcut past the design pass.
- artifact-diagramming: Diagramming know-how for Artifacts - when a picture earns its place, how to draw one that shows the real mechanism, and the inline-SVG mechanics that keep it legible in both themes.
- artifact-capabilities: Runtime capabilities a published Artifact page can be granted — behavior static HTML cannot provide on its own, such as the page reading live or connected data, remembering what people do on it (a poll, a sign-up sheet, a checklist, a document edited in place — it saves new versions of itself), keeping state shared across viewers, knowing who is viewing, asking Claude a question of its own, storing files people add, or handing the viewer a file to save. Serves this user's live capability roster and the typed call definitions. Load it whenever the user asks for an artifact needing any such runtime behavior.
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- code-review: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs and reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups at the given effort level (low/medium: fewer, high-confidence findings; high→max: broader coverage, may include uncertain findings; ultra: deep multi-agent review in the cloud); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. Pass --comment to post findings as inline PR comments, or --fix to apply the findings to the working tree after the review. For ultra on a GitHub.com PR target, --post asks to post the finished review’s findings to the PR as a single comment from the user’s GitHub account (not a review; the launch dialog still confirms in interactive sessions, while non-interactive mode posts on the flag alone) and --no-post hides that option.
- simplify: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled cloud agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring cloud agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Reference for the Claude API / Anthropic SDK — model ids, pricing, params, streaming, tool use, MCP, agents, caching, token counting, model migration.
TRIGGER — read BEFORE opening the target file; don't skip because it "looks like a one-liner" — whenever: the prompt names Claude/Anthropic in any form (Claude, Anthropic, Fable, Opus, Sonnet, Haiku, `anthropic`, `@anthropic-ai`, `claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `[1m]`); the user asks about an LLM (pricing/model choice/limits/caching) — never answer from memory; OR the task is LLM-shaped with provider unstated (agent/MCP/tool-definition/multi-agent/RAG/LLM-judge/computer-use; generate/summarize/extract/classify/rewrite/converse over NL; debugging refusals/cutoffs/streaming/tool-calls/tokens).
SKIP only when another provider is being worked on (overrides all triggers): OpenAI/GPT/Gemini/Llama/Mistral/Cohere/Ollama named in the query; OR `grep -rE 'openai|langchain_openai|google.generativeai|genai|mistralai|cohere|ollama'` over the project hits (run this grep FIRST if no provider named — don't Read the file).
- workflow-authoring: Reference for writing a Workflow tool script (script API and gotchas, resume, quality patterns, worked examples). Load before authoring a script for a workflow the user already opted into; it does not itself authorize running one.
- run: Launch and drive this project's app to see a change working. Use when asked to run, start, or screenshot the app, or to confirm a change works in the real app (not just tests). First looks for a project skill that already covers launching the app; otherwise falls back to built-in patterns per project type (CLI, server, TUI, Electron, browser-driven, library).

1	/**
2	 * Team invitations: consent tokens, plus who is entitled to see whom.
3	 *
4	 * WHY THIS MODULE NO LONGER EXPORTS `requireArea`
5	 * ----------------------------------------------
6	 * It used to export `requireArea(orgId, area)` — a page guard for "org-scoped
7	 * dashboard pages". There were none: `requireArea` had zero call sites in the
8	 * repo (AUDIT-24H rec. 47, QA-PRELAUNCH P1-19), `memberCanAccessHref` was
9	 * referenced only from its own docblock, and `Membership.areas` was write-only.
10	 * Meanwhile the Team UI rendered a checkbox per dashboard area and reported
11	 * "Access updated." So an owner who unticked everything except Invoices was
12	 * shown a restriction that no loader, action or route ever consulted. That is
13	 * the same defect class as the fake SSL certs and the migration that logged 4/4
14	 * with six domains dark, and it is the more dangerous shape of it: a security
15	 * control that reports success while enforcing nothing.
16	 *
17	 * Wiring it up for real would mean org-scoping every dashboard loader and every
18	 * server action that touches a server, domain, volume, invoice or ticket — none
19	 * of which live in this module's blast radius. A half-wired version (nav hidden,
20	 * loaders open) is strictly worse than none, because hiding a nav item looks
21	 * like enforcement. So the area system is deleted rather than faked, and this
22	 * module now carries the two things teams genuinely need in order to be safe.
23	 *
24	 * 1. INVITE TOKENS (consent). `inviteMember` used to create a Membership
25	 *    outright — the invitee never agreed to anything — and the team page then
26	 *    handed the inviter every co-member's `userId` and email. That is precisely
27	 *    the identity feed that made the unauthenticated 2FA oracle
28	 *    (`verifyTotpForUser`, QA-PRELAUNCH P0-2) targetable at a named account:
29	 *    type a victim's email, get back their internal id. Membership now requires
30	 *    the invitee to click Accept while signed in as the invited address.
31	 *
32	 * 2. `canAdministerOrg` — the single definition of "may administer membership",
33	 *    used both to authorise mutations and to decide whether a viewer is
34	 *    entitled to co-members' email addresses.
35	 *
36	 * Plain server-side module (no "use server"), so both the server actions and the
37	 * accept page can import these helpers. Nothing here is client-safe.
38	 */
39	import { createHash } from "node:crypto";
40	import { EncryptJWT, jwtDecrypt } from "jose";
41	
42	/**
43	 * Invitation lifetime. Short on purpose: the token is the entire invitation
44	 * (see below), so expiry is the only thing that eventually retires a link the
45	 * sender regrets.
46	 */
47	export const INVITE_TTL_HOURS = 72;
48	
49	/** What an invitation carries. `invitedBy` is re-checked at accept time. */
50	export type InviteClaims = {
51	  orgId: string;
52	  /** Lowercased email the invitation was addressed to. Binds the link to one person. */
53	  email: string;
54	  role: string;
55	  invitedBy: string;
56	};
57	
58	/**
59	 * 256-bit key for the invite JWE, derived from AUTH_SECRET with an
60	 * invite-specific salt — the same derivation pattern as lib/terminal-token.ts.
61	 * The distinct salt means a session cookie can never be replayed as an
62	 * invitation (or vice-versa) even though both trace back to one secret.
63	 */
64	function inviteKey(): Uint8Array {
65	  const secret = process.env.AUTH_SECRET;
66	  if (!secret) throw new Error("AUTH_SECRET is not set — cannot issue team invitations");
67	  return new Uint8Array(createHash("sha256").update(`nxeon-org-invite:${secret}`).digest());
68	}
69	
70	/**
71	 * Mint an invitation token.
72	 *
73	 * ENCRYPTED (JWE, A256GCM), not merely signed. A signed JWT's payload is
74	 * readable by anyone holding the link, and this payload contains the inviter's
75	 * `userId` — the exact value the 2FA oracle needed (P0-2). An invitation that
76	 * leaked an internal user id to whoever opened the email would reintroduce the
77	 * hole this change exists to close, so the token is opaque to its bearer.
78	 *
79	 * STATELESS by necessity: prisma/schema.prisma has no Invitation model and is
80	 * frozen for this change. The consequences are real and are stated plainly in
81	 * the UI rather than papered over — pending invitations cannot be listed, and
82	 * they cannot be revoked individually. What limits them instead:
83	 *   - they expire (INVITE_TTL_HOURS);
84	 *   - `acceptInvite` re-verifies that the inviter STILL holds OWNER/ADMIN in the
85	 *     org, so demoting or removing an admin voids their outstanding invitations;
86	 *   - they are bound to one email address, so a forwarded link is useless.
87	 * If pending-invite listing/revocation is wanted, that needs a schema field —
88	 * an `Invitation` model (orgId, email, role, invitedById, tokenHash, expiresAt,
89	 * acceptedAt, revokedAt) is the missing piece.
90	 */
91	export async function signInviteToken(claims: InviteClaims): Promise<string> {
92	  return new EncryptJWT({
93	    // `kind` is belt-and-braces on top of the salted key: any token that decrypts
94	    // but wasn't minted here is rejected rather than interpreted.
95	    kind: "org-invite",
96	    orgId: claims.orgId,
97	    email: claims.email,
98	    role: claims.role,
99	    invitedBy: claims.invitedBy,
100	  })
101	    .setProtectedHeader({ alg: "dir", enc: "A256GCM" })
102	    .setIssuedAt()
103	    .setExpirationTime(`${INVITE_TTL_HOURS}h`)
104	    .encrypt(inviteKey());
105	}
106	
107	/**
108	 * Decrypt + validate an invitation token. Returns null for anything that isn't a
109	 * well-formed, unexpired invitation — tampered, truncated, expired, minted with
110	 * a different secret, or a token of some other kind. Never throws, so callers
111	 * can render one honest "invalid or expired" message without leaking which of
112	 * those it was.
113	 */
114	export async function verifyInviteToken(token: string): Promise<InviteClaims | null> {
115	  if (!token) return null;
116	  try {
117	    const { payload } = await jwtDecrypt(token, inviteKey());
118	    if (payload.kind !== "org-invite") return null;
119	    const { orgId, email, role, invitedBy } = payload as Record<string, unknown>;
120	    if (
121	      typeof orgId !== "string" ||
122	      typeof email !== "string" ||
123	      typeof role !== "string" ||
124	      typeof invitedBy !== "string" ||
125	      !orgId ||
126	      !email ||
127	      !role ||
128	      !invitedBy
129	    ) {
130	      return null;
131	    }
132	    return { orgId, email: email.toLowerCase(), role, invitedBy };
133	  } catch {
134	    return null;
135	  }
136	}

138	/**
139	 * Roles that may administer membership (invite / change roles / remove) — and,
140	 * because the two questions have the same answer, the only viewers entitled to
141	 * see co-members' email addresses. A rank-and-file member gets the roster's
142	 * names; harvesting a list of addresses out of an org you were added to is how
143	 * the identity leak above was monetised.
144	 */
145	export function canAdministerOrg(role: string): boolean {
146	  return role === "OWNER" || role === "ADMIN";
147	}

# Nxeon Auth/RBAC/Admin-Access-Control — Investigation Report

## 1. `User` model / `Role` enum — `/opt/nxeon/prisma/schema.prisma`

**`Role` enum** (line 10-15):
```prisma
enum Role {
  CUSTOMER
  SUPPORT
  BILLING
  ADMIN
}
```
So today there are already **4 roles, not 2** — `CUSTOMER`, `SUPPORT`, `BILLING`, `ADMIN`. `SUPPORT`/`BILLING` are "partial staff" roles. `ADMIN` is a superuser that implicitly passes every area check (see §3).

**`User` model** (starts line 98): relevant fields:
- `role Role @default(CUSTOMER)` (line 133) — the only role/permission field on `User` itself. No `area`, `permissions`, `canAccess` column on the model — access granularity is computed in code from `role`, not stored per-user.
- `discordUserId String? @unique` (line 132) — staff Discord-account link (see §6). **Not yet pushed to prod DB** per the comment (lines 111-131) — every read/write goes through `as any` casts until `prisma db push` is run for real.
- `googleId String? @unique` (line 108) — "Login with Google" identity link, same nullable/unique pattern.
- `suspended Boolean` (line 135), `sessionVersion Int @default(0)` (line 175), `totpEnabled Boolean` (line 176) — used by session validity/2FA enforcement, not access-area logic.
- `excludeFromRevenue Boolean` (line 139) — unrelated (metrics-only, marks owner/test/staff accounts).

**No per-user IP field exists anywhere on `User`.** There is no `ipHash`, `allowlist`, or per-staff IP column in the schema at all — confirmed by grep of the whole schema.

**`AuditLog` model** (line 870-877):
```prisma
model AuditLog {
  id        String   @id @default(cuid())
  userId    String?
  user      User?    @relation(fields: [userId], references: [id])
  action    String
  detail    String?
  createdAt DateTime @default(now())
}
```
Minimal — just actor (`userId`, nullable = "system"), a free-text `action` string, optional `detail` string, timestamp. No `ip`, `area`, or `resource` column.

## 2. `lib/auth.ts` — session, staff helpers, impersonation, IP restriction

Full file at `/opt/nxeon/lib/auth.ts` (248 lines). Key exports:

- **Session cookie**: `nxeon_session` (HS256 JWT via `jose`, configurable name via `NXEON_COOKIE_NAME`), payload `{ sub: userId, sv: sessionVersion, typ: "session" }`. Lifetime is admin-configurable (`session_length_days` setting, default 30). A separate non-httpOnly `nxeon_authed` cookie flags "signed in" for the static marketing header only.
- **`requireUser()`** (line 223-227): resolves `currentUser()` (which folds in impersonation), throws `UNAUTHORIZED` if none.
- **`requireAdmin()`** (line 229-233): `requireUser()` + throws `FORBIDDEN` unless `role === "ADMIN"` exactly. **Flat boolean check — no area concept.**
- **`requireStaff()`** (line 240-247): new-ish helper, uses `realUser()` (ignores impersonation), allows `SUPPORT | BILLING | ADMIN`. Docblock explicitly says: *"Fine-grained per-area gating lives in lib/rbac.ts (`requireArea`)"* — confirming the area system is the intended finer-grained layer on top of this.
- **Impersonation** (lines 111-221): real, working mechanism.
  - `setImpersonation(targetUserId)` — ADMIN-only, mints a separate `nxeon_session_imp` JWT (`typ: "imp"`, 2h TTL, embeds `adminId`), refuses to target another ADMIN.
  - `currentUser()` — returns the impersonated target if a valid grant exists and re-validates target isn't suspended/promoted-to-ADMIN since mint time.
  - `impersonating()` — returns `{ admin, target }` or null; used to show the "impersonating" banner and to attribute audit-log entries (`actingAdmin=<id>` appended to `detail`, see §5).
  - `assertNotImpersonating()` — guard for money-moving actions.
  - `typ` discriminator prevents a session token and an impersonation token from being interchangeable even though both are signed with the same `AUTH_SECRET` (documented CVE-style writeup in the docblock, lines 56-84).

- **IP restriction — EXISTS, but only as one global admin-wide allowlist**, not per-staff and not in `lib/auth.ts`. It lives in `/opt/nxeon/app/admin/layout.tsx` (lines 26-58):
  - `adminIpBlocked()` reads the `allowed_admin_ips` setting (comma-separated literal IPs, stored via `lib/settings.ts` / editable at `/admin/settings`, see `lib/actions-settings.ts:293`), trusts `X-Real-IP` / last hop of `X-Forwarded-For` from nginx, and **fails open** (allows access) if the list is empty, malformed, or the IP can't be determined.
  - This is applied to **every staff member identically** — there is no per-user/per-role IP list, just one global list for the whole `/admin` surface.
  - `adminHostBlocked()` (lines 10-16) is a separate, coarser gate: `/admin` 404s entirely unless the request `Host` header is in `NXEON_ADMIN_HOSTS` — i.e. the admin portal is already expected to be served from a dedicated hostname distinct from the public site. This is a good foundation for point (c) — a separate employee portal.
  - Grep confirms **no other** `ipHash`/`clientIp`/`allowlist`/`whitelist` results relate to auth/admin restriction — the other ~30 hits (`app/api/_lib/client-ip.ts`, `lib/rate-limit.ts`) are all rate-limiting / promo-fraud (`firstMonthFreeEligible`) infrastructure, reusable as the IP-extraction primitive (`clientIp()`/`trustedClientIp()`) but not currently wired to any per-user allow/deny logic.

## 3. `canAccess` / `requireArea` — a real, already-working per-section RBAC layer: `/opt/nxeon/lib/rbac.ts` (155 lines, full file read)

This directly answers the central question: **a genuine per-section admin permission system already exists** — it is not a flat ADMIN/CUSTOMER boolean plus "a couple of hardcoded areas." It's a small but complete and heavily-used RBAC layer:

```ts
export type Area =
  | "overview" | "analytics" | "clients" | "support"
  | "fleet" | "billing" | "accounting" | "platform";

export const AREA_ROLES: Record<Area, Role[]> = {
  overview: ["SUPPORT", "BILLING", "ADMIN"],
  analytics: ["ADMIN"],
  clients: ["SUPPORT", "ADMIN"],
  support: ["SUPPORT", "ADMIN"],
  fleet: ["ADMIN"],
  billing: ["BILLING", "ADMIN"],
  accounting: ["ADMIN"],
  platform: ["ADMIN"],
};

export function canAccess(role: Role, area: Area): boolean {
  return role === "ADMIN" || AREA_ROLES[area].includes(role);
}
export function isStaff(role: Role): boolean {
  return role === "SUPPORT" || role === "BILLING" || role === "ADMIN";
}
```

**The 8 exact area strings in use today: `overview`, `analytics`, `clients`, `support`, `fleet`, `billing`, `accounting`, `platform`.** (Confirmed identical set via `requireArea(...)` grep across ~330 call sites — every literal used is one of these 8; no other area string appears anywhere in the codebase.)

Other pieces of `lib/rbac.ts`:
- `HREF_AREA: Record<string, Area>` (lines 48-133) — a hand-maintained map from every admin route prefix to its governing area (used for nav visibility, default `"platform"` for anything unmapped).
- `areaForHref(href)` / `canAccessHref(role, href)` — used by `app/admin/layout.tsx` to filter the nav to only areas a role can reach.
- `requireArea(area): Promise<User>` (lines 148-154) — the actual server-side page guard: redirects to `/login` if signed out, `/dashboard` if not staff, `/admin` if staff but wrong area; otherwise returns the real user (bypasses impersonation deliberately).

**Scale of adoption**: `requireArea(...)` is called from ~85+ admin page files and ~30 `lib/actions-*.ts` server-action files (grep returned 300+ call sites), almost always as the *first line* of the page/action, frequently re-checked inside every individual server action even when the parent page already gated it (explicit defense-in-depth pattern called out in comments, e.g. `lib/actions-backups-admin.ts:25`, `lib/actions-hosting.ts`, `lib/actions-abuse.ts`). `canAccess(role, area)` is also called directly (not via the redirect-throwing `requireArea`) in ~10 places that need a boolean rather than a redirect (API routes like `app/api/admin/chat-unread/route.ts`, `app/api/admin/monitor-feed/route.ts`, and `lib/discord-bridge.ts` for validating a Discord-linked staff member still holds support access).

**Important caveat — `lib/team-guard.ts`** (customer-facing org/team feature, unrelated to admin) used to have its *own*, differently-scoped `requireArea(orgId, area)` for customer team member dashboard permissions. It was **deliberately deleted** (long docblock at lines 1-38) because it had zero real call sites and gave a false impression of enforcement (nav hid items but no loader/action actually checked them). This is a useful cautionary precedent: when extending granular access control, half-wiring it (hiding nav only) was explicitly treated as a security regression worse than not having the control, and was ripped out rather than left. Any new granular admin ACL work should heed this — a UI checkbox must always be backed by a real server-side check on every corresponding action/loader, not just nav filtering.

**Conclusion for planning purposes**: You are NOT starting from scratch for (a)/(b). `Role` enum already has room for staff sub-roles (`SUPPORT`, `BILLING`) and `lib/rbac.ts`'s `Area`/`AREA_ROLES`/`canAccess`/`requireArea` is exactly the mechanism to extend — add new `Role` enum values (e.g. `MODERATOR`, `MARKETER`, whatever staff roles you need) and slot them into `AREA_ROLES`, and/or add new `Area` values for finer granularity than the current 8 buckets. The one gap: **the model is role→area** (coarse, ~8 static roles × 8 areas), not user→area — there's no way today to grant one specific `SUPPORT` staffer more/fewer areas than every other `SUPPORT` staffer without inventing a new role for them. If you need true per-employee (not per-role) granularity, that's the actual new work — e.g. a `StaffAreaGrant` join table or a `permissions: Area[]` field, with `canAccess`/`requireArea` updated to check it instead of/in addition to `AREA_ROLES[role]`.

## 4. `app/admin/layout.tsx` — nav construction, `lib/admin-groups.ts` — full admin destination list

`/opt/nxeon/app/admin/layout.tsx` (221 lines, read in full):
- Gate order: `adminHostBlocked()` → 404 if wrong hostname → `realUser()` → redirect `/login` → `isStaff()` check → redirect `/dashboard` → refuse if impersonating → `adminIpBlocked()` global-IP-allowlist gate (renders "Access restricted" page, not a redirect) → optional `enforce_staff_2fa` setting redirect to `/dashboard/settings?require2fa=1` if staff has no TOTP.
- Nav is built from `ADMIN_NAV` (see `/opt/nxeon/lib/admin-groups.ts`), **already varies by role**: `visibleSections` (lines 112-128) filters every entry's `tabs` down to `canAccessHref(user.role, tab.href)`, drops empty entries/sections, and computes `allowedHrefs` fed into `<AdminSubTabs allowed={allowedHrefs}>` so in-page sub-tab bars hide the same items the sidebar does. Two additional feature flags (`feature_admin_agency`, `feature_admin_ads`) can hide whole sections independent of role.
- Badges (unread counts) are separately computed per route (chat, tickets, abuse, feedback, improvements, cold-email inbox).

**Full admin destination list** — `lib/admin-groups.ts`'s `ADMIN_NAV` documents ~85 routes across 10 top-level sections (`start`, `customers`, `fleet`, `revenue`, `accounting`, `marketing`, `coldemail`, `agency`, `ads`, `mail`, `platform`). Notable entries relevant to the user's follow-up items:
- **Customers → Support**: Tickets (`/admin/support`), Live chat (`/admin/chat`), Feedback (`/admin/feedback`).
- **Customers → Clients**: Clients (`/admin/users`), Organizations (`/admin/orgs`).
- **Mail** (its own top-level section): Inbox (`/admin/inbox`), Deliverability (`/admin/mail`), Mailboxes (`/admin/mailboxes`), Email templates (`/admin/email-templates`).
- **Marketing → Reddit**: Post templates (`/admin/reddit`).
- **Platform → Settings**: Settings, Automation, **Staff** (`/admin/staff`), Logs, **Audit** (`/admin/audit`).

This file is the single source of truth for both the sidebar and `HREF_AREA` in `lib/rbac.ts` — any new page needs an entry here (for nav) plus a mapping in `HREF_AREA` (for area gating) plus its own `requireArea(...)` call.

## 5. `AuditLog` / `audit()` helper / audit UI

- **`audit()` helper**: `/opt/nxeon/lib/actions.ts:81-88`:
  ```ts
  async function audit(userId: string | null, action: string, detail?: string) {
    const imp = await impersonating();
    const actor = imp ? `actingAdmin=${imp.admin.id}` : "";
    const fullDetail = detail && actor ? `${detail} ${actor}` : detail || actor || undefined;
    await db.auditLog.create({ data: { userId, action, detail: fullDetail } });
  }
  ```
  It's **private/unexported**, used only within `lib/actions.ts` (5 call sites: `user.register`, `user.login`, `server.<action>`, `wallet.topup`, and one more). It is **not** a shared, codebase-wide audit primitive — most `lib/actions-*.ts` files (there are ~9 files that reference "audit(" per the earlier grep) do their own direct `db.auditLog.create({...})` calls rather than importing a shared helper (confirmed: `lib/actions-staff.ts:31` calls `db.auditLog.create` directly for `staff.setRole`). So audit logging coverage is inconsistent/ad hoc — some admin mutations log, many likely don't; there's no single enforced "every state-changing admin action must audit()" convention. **This is worth flagging for the plan**: if per-page/IP access control is added, you likely want a single shared `audit()`/`auditAdmin()` helper that all admin actions funnel through, rather than continuing the current pattern of scattered direct `db.auditLog.create` calls.
  - The impersonation-attribution trick (`detail += " actingAdmin=<id>"`) is a workaround for the schema having no explicit "acting as" column — worth reconsidering if you add a real audit rework (e.g. add `actingUserId` as its own column instead of string-encoding it into `detail`).

- **Audit viewer UI**: **Yes, it exists** — `/opt/nxeon/app/admin/audit/page.tsx` (`requireArea("platform")`, ADMIN-only). Lists latest 200 `AuditLog` rows with columns Time / Actor / Action / Detail, resolves `actingAdmin=<id>` markers out of `detail` to show the real actor + an "impersonating X" badge (this correctly-attributing logic was itself a bug fix, per the large comment at lines 17-34 of that file).

## 6. Staff identity — Discord OAuth linking (already exists, currently in-flight/not-yet-migrated)

- `User.discordUserId` (schema.prisma line 132) is a nullable-unique field storing the real Discord snowflake a staff member has proven ownership of via Discord OAuth. **Per the schema comment, this column has NOT been pushed to production Postgres yet** — every read/write in code goes through `as any` casts (confirmed in `lib/discord-bridge.ts:286` doing `db.user.findUnique({ where: { discordUserId } as any, ... })`).
- Flow: `/opt/nxeon/lib/discord-oauth.ts` implements a standard OAuth2 Authorization Code flow scoped to `identify` only, using a **separate Discord app credential** from the bot token used elsewhere (`lib/discord.ts`). CSRF `state` is a short-lived signed JWT (10 min, `AUTH_SECRET`-derived, distinct `typ` from session/impersonation tokens) embedding the initiating staff user's id — but the callback route (`app/api/admin/discord/callback/route.ts`) re-derives the actual actor from `requireArea("support")` (the real session) and only uses `state`'s uid to *confirm* a match, never as authority — same defensive pattern as session vs. impersonation tokens.
- Purpose: lets Nxeon reply to customer support threads that bridge to Discord, correctly attributed to the individual staff member who replied (`lib/discord-bridge.ts`'s `submitDiscordReply`, which re-validates `canAccess(linkedUser.role, "support")` at reply time so a demoted/former staffer's old Discord link stops working immediately even if the row isn't deleted).
- **Relevance to a broader staff-identity system**: this Discord link is purely an *auxiliary* identity binding for one feature (Discord support bridge) — staff still authenticate primarily via the normal `nxeon_session` cookie (password/Google OAuth login, same as customers, just gated by `role`). There is **no SSO/staff-specific login page** — `/opt/nxeon/app/login/page.tsx` is the single login surface for both customers and staff; staff are just accounts whose `role` happens to be `SUPPORT`/`BILLING`/`ADMIN`. So "half of what's needed for a broader staff-identity system" is accurate only in a narrow sense (per-person external-account linking pattern, OAuth plumbing, JWT-state CSRF pattern) — the actual staff *authentication* path (login, session, 2FA) is unified with customers, not separate. A genuine "employee portal" with its own identity provider would be new work, though the `NXEON_ADMIN_HOSTS` host-gate (§2) and the existing separate `nxeon_session_imp` token pattern are reusable scaffolding.

## 7. Specific admin pages requested — exact paths and current gating

| Feature | File(s) | Current gate |
|---|---|---|
| Tickets (support) | `/opt/nxeon/app/admin/support/page.tsx`, `/opt/nxeon/app/admin/support/[id]/page.tsx` | `requireArea("support")` — reachable by `SUPPORT` and `ADMIN` |
| Reddit marketing templates | `/opt/nxeon/app/admin/reddit/page.tsx` | `requireArea("platform")` — **ADMIN-only** (despite being marketing content, not fleet/platform-sensitive — a candidate for a new, less-restrictive area under your planned granular system) |
| Admin-side inbox/mail (company webmail) | `/opt/nxeon/app/admin/inbox/page.tsx` | `requireArea("platform")` — ADMIN-only (comment explicitly says "ADMIN-only via requireArea('platform')") |
| Mail deliverability dashboard | `/opt/nxeon/app/admin/mail/page.tsx` | `requireArea("platform")` — ADMIN-only |
| Mailboxes (create/manage company mailboxes) | `/opt/nxeon/app/admin/mailboxes/page.tsx` | `requireArea("platform")` — ADMIN-only |
| Clients/customers list | `/opt/nxeon/app/admin/users/page.tsx`, `/opt/nxeon/app/admin/users/[id]/page.tsx` | `requireArea("clients")` — `SUPPORT` and `ADMIN`, **but** the page itself further restricts mutating actions (Impersonate, Suspend, bulk suspend) to `me.role === "ADMIN"` client-side gating on top of the area check, since those specific server actions (`lib/actions-admin-billing.ts`) are `requireAdmin()`-gated, not just `requireArea`. **Per-page admin access control already exists in real, enforced form** via `lib/rbac.ts`'s `Area` / `AREA_ROLES` / `canAccess` / `requireArea`, used at ~85+ admin pages and ~30 action files. It is **not** a flat ADMIN/CUSTOMER boolean — there are 4 roles (`CUSTOMER`, `SUPPORT`, `BILLING`, `ADMIN`) mapped onto 8 areas (`overview`, `analytics`, `clients`, `support`, `fleet`, `billing`, `accounting`, `platform`), with nav visibility, route guards, and (in `/admin/users`) even in-page action-level checks layered on top. However, granularity today is **role-level, not user-level** — every `SUPPORT` employee gets identically all "support"/"overview"/"clients" areas; there's no way to grant one specific employee a custom subset. Most non-fleet/non-billing content (Mail, Marketing, Reddit, Settings, Automation, Logs, Improvements, Boards, Cold Email, Agency, Ads — essentially everything mapped to `"platform"`) is currently lumped as ADMIN-only regardless of actual sensitivity, which is the real headroom for your planned finer-grained system.

For IP whitelisting: a **global, admin-portal-wide** IP allowlist already exists (`allowed_admin_ips` setting, enforced in `app/admin/layout.tsx`, fails open) — but there is **no per-staff-member** IP restriction anywhere; that would be entirely new (a per-user IP list/column plus a per-user check in the same layout gate, likely reusing `lib/rate-limit.ts`'s `clientIp()` IP-extraction primitive).

For staff identity: Discord OAuth account-linking exists (`User.discordUserId`, not yet migrated to prod) but is a narrow, single-feature (support-bridge reply attribution) identity binding layered on top of the same unified customer/staff login — there is no separate staff authentication system or employee portal today; `NXEON_ADMIN_HOSTS` (host-based 404 gate) is the only existing "separate portal" infrastructure to build on.
